'''''Ophrys sphegodes''''', commonly known as the '''early spider-orchid''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007|access-date=17 October 2014   }}</ref> is a species of sexually-deceptive [[orchid]] (through [[Pouyannian mimicry]]) native to Europe and the Middle East. It is a highly varied species with many subspecies recognised.

==Description==

Plant height varies with latitude. In the UK the maximum height is around {{Convert|20|cm|abbr=on|sigfig=1}}, but around the Mediterranean a height of {{Convert|70|cm|abbr=on}} may be reached.<ref name="First Nature - Ophrys sphegodes">[https://www.first-nature.com/flowers/ophrys-sphegodes.php First Nature – Ophrys sphegodes]</ref> Flowers March–May<ref name="First Nature - Ophrys sphegodes"/> (April–May in northern latitudes). Each shoot may carry between 2 and 18 flowers.
The flowers have yellow-green [[sepal]]s and a velvety red-brown labellum with a distinctive silvery-blue '''H''' marking so that the flowers much resemble an [[arthropod]] and especially a spider.

Similar to ''[[Ophrys fuciflora]]'' and ''[[Ophrys apifera]]'' but flowers differ in that late spider orchid and bee orchid have much smaller petals than sepals; in early spider orchid petals and sepals are a similar size. They are also distinguished by patches of colour on the labellum; late spider orchid has a yellow point at the centre of the distal end of the labellum, while bee orchid has a red patch at the proximal end of the labellum.

==Distribution and habitat==

Found on unimproved [[alkaline]] meadows, woodland edges,<ref name="First Nature - Ophrys sphegodes"/> as well as slopes, banks<ref>[https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Ophrys+sphegodes Plants for a Future – Ophrys sphegodes]</ref> and waste land. It is widespread across most of Europe and the middle East from Britain south to Portugal and east to Iran.<ref name="asdfqw4t524">[http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=141753 Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]</ref>

In [[Great Britain|Britain]], it is restricted to parts of [[Dorset]], Hampshire, [[Kent]] and [[Sussex]] and is regarded as rare although where it is found it may be in stands of many hundreds of plants. It is classified as a British [[IUCN Red List|Red Data Book]] plant. Despite its apparent vulnerability, it has very successfully colonised the chalk spoil dumping grounds created near Dover at [[Samphire Hoe]] from the excavations of the [[Channel Tunnel]]. Worldwide, the IUCN conservation status of this species is least concern as of 2018.<ref>[https://eunis.eea.europa.eu/species/189719 European Environment Agency – Ophrys sphegodes Mill.]</ref><ref>{{British Red Data Books|volume=1}}</ref>

==Ecology==

In the UK ''Ophrys sphegodes'' is pollinated by the miner bee ''[[Andrena nigroaenea]]'',<ref>{{Cite news |last=Barkham |first=Patrick |date=5 April 2018 |title=Climate change threatens rare British orchid that tricks bees into mating |language=en-GB |work=The Guardian |url=https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2018/apr/05/climate-change-threatens-rare-british-orchid-that-tricks-bees-into-mating |access-date=21 April 2023 |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> a polylectic pollinator (i.e. one that visits many different species of flower), a bee species which requires dry sandy soils.<ref>{{Cite web |last=NatureSpot |title=Andrena nigroaenea  |url=https://www.naturespot.org.uk/species/andrena-nigroaenea |access-date=21 April 2023 |website=www.naturespot.org.uk}}Nature Spot – Andrena nigroaenea]</ref> Different subspecies have evolved to attract different pollinators.<ref name="First Nature - Ophrys sphegodes"/>

This orchid species is able to form [[symbiotic]] relationships with a range of species of [[mycorrhizal fungi]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jacquemyn |first1=Hans |last2=Brys |first2=Rein |last3=Waud |first3=Michael |last4=Busschaert |first4=Pieter |last5=Lievens |first5=Bart |date=May 2015 |title=Mycorrhizal networks and coexistence in species‐rich orchid communities |journal=New Phytologist |language=en |volume=206 |issue=3 |pages=1127–1134 |doi=10.1111/nph.13281 |pmid=25614926 |doi-access=free |issn=0028-646X}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==

''Ophrys'' comes from the [[Ancient Greek]] for eyebrow, perhaps a reference to the velvety brown appearance of the labellum. ''Sphegodes'' comes from the Ancient Greek for wasp-like.<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=YsUpDwAAQBAJ&dq=sphegodes+latin+greek&pg=PP21 The Orchid Hunter – A Young Botanist's Search for Happiness]</ref><ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=NJ6PyhVuecwC&dq=sphegodes+latin+greek&pg=PA358 The Names of Plants]</ref> This species was formerly called ''O. aranifera'', meaning spider-carrying.

The genus ''Ophrys'' is the most species-rich (i.e. diverse) genus of orchids in Europe and the Mediterranean with over 200 species, according to ''Orchids of Britain and Europe'' by Pierre Delforge.
